practices.name: Social Impact & Community
practices.meta_description: Social impact and community consulting: strategy, theory of change, stakeholder engagement, philanthropy and public sector work grounded in evidence.
practices.tagline: Evidence-based strategy for organizations accountable to communities, not only to balance sheets.
intro: The Social Impact & Community practice helps foundations, nonprofits, public agencies and companies design, deliver and measure work that changes conditions for people outside their walls. We build social impact strategies, theories of change, engagement processes, philanthropic portfolios and workforce programs that hold up under scrutiny from boards, funders, residents and regulators. Our work sits where good intentions meet operational reality: the program that must scale without losing fidelity, the corporate commitment that must survive a leadership change, the public service that must reach the residents it was designed for.

We lead with people because social outcomes are produced by people. A workforce program succeeds when employers, training providers and learners each see a reason to stay engaged. A community investment lasts when residents shaped it and can see their priorities in it. A grant strategy works when grantees can report honestly about what is and is not working. Our Listen, Measure, Design, Deliver, Sustain method treats those relationships as the core of the strategy, not a consultation step added at the end.

We also hold impact work to the same evidentiary standard as any other investment decision. That means separating outputs from outcomes, naming assumptions, choosing indicators that can be collected without burdening the people being served, and building learning systems that help leaders change course when the evidence points somewhere unexpected. Rigor and humility are not in tension; together they are what make impact claims credible to the people who fund, govern and depend on the work.

themes.title: Outcomes over outputs
themes.body: Counting workshops held or dollars granted is easy. Demonstrating that conditions changed for people is harder and more important. We help clients build logic models and measurement frameworks that distinguish activities, outputs, outcomes and long-term impact, so that reports to boards and funders describe real change and acknowledge contribution rather than overstating attribution.

themes.title: Power-aware participation
themes.body: Engagement is only as credible as the influence it offers. Using frameworks such as the IAP2 Spectrum of Public Participation, we help clients decide honestly whether they are informing, consulting, involving, collaborating with or empowering communities, and then design processes, compensation and feedback loops that match that promise.

themes.title: Durable institutions
themes.body: Impact depends on organizations that can sustain it. We strengthen the governance, operating models, partnerships and talent systems behind mission-driven work, so that strategies outlast a single grant cycle, executive tenure or political term, and so that staff closest to communities have the capacity and authority to act on what they learn.

practices.name: Strategy & Operations
practices.meta_description: Strategy and operations consulting that puts people at the center: strategic planning, operating models, process improvement, customer, AI and talent strategy.
practices.tagline: Strategy and operations that work because the people who run them helped build them.
intro: The Strategy & Operations practice helps leadership teams set direction and build the organization that can deliver it. We work on strategic plans, operating models, process improvement, customer and innovation strategy, responsible AI adoption and talent strategy for companies, investor-backed businesses, nonprofits and public institutions. The common thread is execution: most strategies fail not because the analysis was wrong but because decision rights, workflows, incentives and capabilities were never redesigned to support them.

Our people lens is practical rather than sentimental. Every operating model is a set of decisions about who does what work, with what information, under whose authority. Every process improvement changes someone's day. Every AI deployment shifts tasks, skills and judgment between people and systems. We start by listening to the employees and customers who live inside those systems, measure where value and friction actually sit, and design changes with the people who will have to run them.

The result is strategy that is explicit about trade-offs, operations that are simpler to work within, and organizations that can adapt as conditions change. We bring the analytical discipline of a strategy firm and the implementation patience of an operating partner, and we hand over the dashboards, governance routines and internal capability needed to sustain progress after our engagement ends.

themes.title: Strategy that reaches the front line
themes.body: A plan that lives in a board deck changes little. We translate strategic choices into priorities, objectives and key results, resource allocation and management routines that middle managers can use, and we test the plan with the employees and customers who will experience it before it is finalized.

themes.title: Operations designed around people
themes.body: We map how work actually flows, from customer request to delivery, using value stream mapping and service blueprinting to find handoffs, rework and waiting. Improvements are designed with frontline teams, which tends to produce changes that stick and surfaces the practical knowledge that never appears in a process manual.

themes.title: Responsible adoption of new technology
themes.body: AI and automation are operating model decisions, not only technology decisions. We help leaders choose use cases, set governance, assess workforce impact and plan reskilling and job redesign, so that productivity gains do not come at the cost of trust, fairness or the institutional knowledge that employees carry.

services.name: Social Impact Strategy
services.meta_description: Social impact strategy consulting that links purpose to evidence: focused outcome priorities, logic models, measurement and governance your board can trust.
services.summary: Define where your organization can create meaningful social change, what it will take, and how you will know it is working.
services.lede: Our social impact strategy consulting helps leaders choose focused outcome priorities, align resources and partnerships behind them, and build the evidence to show stakeholders that the work is changing conditions for people.
challenge: Many organizations carry a portfolio of well-intended commitments that grew one decision at a time: a signature program here, a partnership there, a pledge made during a moment of public attention. Each makes sense on its own, but together they rarely add up to a coherent strategy. Boards ask what the organization is actually achieving, funders and investors request evidence the organization cannot produce, and staff spread across too many priorities to do any of them well. The result is activity that is hard to explain and harder to defend.

The people problem underneath is just as serious. Communities that were promised partnership often experience extraction instead: surveys without follow-up, pilots that end when funding does. Employees who joined for the mission lose confidence when impact claims outpace reality. Leaders sense the gap but lack a shared language to make trade-offs, so decisions default to whoever argues hardest or whichever initiative has the most visible sponsor. A credible social impact strategy has to repair those relationships as well as clarify the plan.

approach.title: Mapping what you do and what others need
approach.body: We interview leaders, staff, partners, funders and community members, and review existing programs, grants and commitments. The aim is to understand the problem from the perspective of the people experiencing it, where your organization has genuine standing to act, and where community expectations differ from internal assumptions about your role and contribution.

approach.title: Baselining assets, gaps and evidence
approach.body: We inventory current investments against outcomes, assess the strength of existing evidence, and scan the landscape of other actors working on the same issues. A materiality and contribution analysis shows where your resources, expertise and relationships are most likely to change outcomes, and where you would add little beyond what others already provide well.

approach.title: Choosing focus and building the logic
approach.body: With a cross-functional working group and community advisors, we set a small number of outcome priorities, test them against your capabilities, and build a logic model for each that links activities to outputs, short-term outcomes and long-term impact, with assumptions and risks stated plainly enough to be tested.

approach.title: Aligning resources, roles and partners
approach.body: We translate priorities into a multiyear roadmap, budget reallocation, governance structure and partner model. That includes deciding what to stop or sunset responsibly, clarifying decision rights between leadership and program teams, and preparing managers and partners to explain the strategy in their own words to staff, grantees and residents.

approach.title: Measuring, learning and reporting
approach.body: We set up an impact measurement framework with a manageable set of indicators, data collection that respects participants' time, and a learning cadence where leaders review evidence and adjust. Board and public reporting templates distinguish contribution from attribution, so the organization can report progress honestly and stand behind its claims.

deliverables: Stakeholder and community listening synthesis
Portfolio inventory mapped to outcomes and evidence strength
Prioritized outcome areas with explicit trade-off rationale
Logic model and assumptions register for each priority
Multiyear roadmap, budget alignment and governance charter
Impact measurement framework and board reporting template
outcomes: A focused set of outcome priorities that leaders, staff and partners can explain consistently.
Resources concentrated where the organization has the strongest standing and evidence to contribute.
Impact reporting that boards, funders and communities regard as credible and candid.
A regular learning rhythm that informs decisions rather than only satisfying compliance requests.
services.who_we_serve: We work with chief executives, chief impact and sustainability officers, foundation presidents, nonprofit boards and executive directors, and investor-backed companies with a stated mission. Typical trigger moments include a new chief executive or board chair, a strategic plan refresh, a major gift or endowment change, rising pressure from investors or regulators for impact evidence, or a recognition that the current portfolio of commitments has grown too diffuse to manage, explain or fund well.
services.impact_lens: A focused social impact strategy changes more than a report. Communities receive sustained commitment instead of short pilots, and they gain a real voice in setting priorities. Employees see a clear connection between their work and the mission, which supports engagement and retention. Customers and partners can trust the organization's claims. And because the strategy is built on evidence and honest trade-offs, scarce resources go further toward the social good the organization exists to advance.

faqs.q: What does a social impact strategy consultant do?
faqs.a: A social impact strategy consultant helps an organization decide which social outcomes to pursue, how its programs, investments and partnerships will contribute to them, and how progress will be measured. The work combines research with affected communities, analysis of existing activity and evidence, facilitated priority setting with leadership, and the design of governance and measurement so the strategy can be managed, reported and improved over time.

faqs.q: How is social impact strategy different from CSR?
faqs.a: Corporate social responsibility often describes a company's broader conduct and commitments, including ethics, environmental practices and community giving. Social impact strategy is narrower and more outcome-focused: it asks which specific changes in people's lives or conditions the organization will work toward, through what causal pathways, and with what evidence. Many companies use social impact strategy to give their CSR program sharper focus and more credible measurement.

faqs.q: How long does a social impact strategy engagement take?
faqs.a: Timelines depend on the size of the portfolio and the depth of community engagement required. A focused strategy for a single business unit or foundation program moves faster than an enterprise-wide redesign with multiple community advisory processes. We agree on scope and milestones at the outset, and we design the engagement so that early findings inform decisions while the full strategy is still being developed.

faqs.q: How do you measure social impact without overburdening programs?
faqs.a: We start with the decisions leaders actually need to make and choose the fewest indicators that inform them. Where possible we use administrative data already collected, sample rather than survey everyone, and pair quantitative indicators with periodic qualitative evidence. Participants and frontline staff help select what is measured, which improves data quality and ensures measurement is useful to the people delivering and receiving services.

services.name: Community Engagement
services.meta_description: Community engagement consulting that gives residents real influence: IAP2-informed design, inclusive outreach, compensated co-design and visible report-backs.
services.summary: Design engagement that gives residents real influence, builds trust over time and produces decisions communities recognize as their own.
services.lede: Our community engagement consulting helps organizations design participation that is honest about the influence it offers, reaches people who are usually left out, and turns what residents say into decisions they can see.
challenge: Organizations that affect a place, whether a hospital system, a developer, a utility, a school district or a city agency, are expected to engage the community. Too often that means a public meeting at an inconvenient hour, a survey that reaches the usual voices, and a summary report that nobody acts on. Residents learn that participation changes little, attendance falls, and the organization concludes that the community is disengaged. Meanwhile projects encounter opposition late, when changes are most expensive and relationships are hardest to repair.

The underlying problem is a mismatch between what engagement promises and what it delivers. Leaders rarely decide in advance how much influence residents will actually have, so expectations diverge. Engagement teams lack the time, budget or language access to reach renters, shift workers, young people, immigrants or people with disabilities. And there is no feedback loop telling participants what happened to their input. Community engagement consulting must address the design of the decision itself, not only the format of the meetings.

approach.title: Understanding history, place and trust
approach.body: Before designing anything, we learn the history of the relationship between your organization and the community, including past promises and grievances. We conduct interviews with community leaders, trusted messengers and frontline staff, and attend existing community gatherings rather than convening new ones, so we understand how people already organize, communicate and decide.

approach.title: Mapping who is affected and who is heard
approach.body: We compare the demographics and geography of past participants with the population affected by the decision, identifying gaps in reach by language, age, tenure, disability and income. We also assess current engagement practices against the IAP2 Spectrum of Public Participation to see where stated intentions and actual influence diverge.

approach.title: Matching the method to the promise
approach.body: With leadership, we decide which decisions are open, what level of participation is appropriate for each, and what constraints are fixed. We then co-design methods with community partners: compensated advisory groups, small-group conversations hosted by local organizations, multilingual and accessible formats, and deliberative sessions where residents weigh real trade-offs with real information.

approach.title: Running engagement and closing the loop
approach.body: We facilitate or support delivery of the engagement, train staff to host conversations well, and partner with community-based organizations who are compensated for their role. Every phase ends with a report back that shows participants what was heard, what changed as a result and, where input was not adopted, why.

approach.title: Building lasting engagement capacity
approach.body: We help institutionalize engagement through standards, a participation policy, a community feedback tracker and an internal community of practice. Where appropriate we support standing advisory bodies or community benefit agreements, so engagement becomes an ongoing relationship with accountability rather than a series of disconnected project consultations.

deliverables: Community context and relationship history assessment
Participation gap analysis by geography and demographics
Engagement plan mapped to the IAP2 participation spectrum
Co-designed engagement toolkit with accessible, multilingual materials
Report-back summaries showing how input shaped decisions
Engagement standards, policy and community feedback tracker
outcomes: Residents who are usually absent from decisions take part and see their influence reflected.
Fewer late-stage objections because concerns surface early, when plans can still change.
Clear, shared expectations about which decisions are open to community influence and how.
Staff who can plan and host respectful engagement without relying on outside facilitators.
services.who_we_serve: We serve community relations and government affairs leaders, public agency directors, hospital community benefit teams, real estate and infrastructure developers, utilities, school districts and foundations working in place-based initiatives. Engagements often begin when a major capital project, rezoning, facility closure, community health needs assessment or rate case requires public input, when prior engagement has damaged trust, or when leaders recognize that their current approach consistently hears from the same small group of voices.
services.impact_lens: Good community engagement improves decisions and the relationships around them. Residents gain real influence over changes to their neighborhoods and services, and they are compensated for their expertise rather than asked to give it freely. Employees in community-facing roles gain the skills and authority to build trust. Projects designed with community input tend to fit local needs better, face less opposition and serve residents more equitably, which benefits both the organization and the place it serves.

faqs.q: What is the IAP2 Spectrum of Public Participation?
faqs.a: The IAP2 Spectrum, developed by the International Association for Public Participation, describes five levels of public influence: inform, consult, involve, collaborate and empower. Each level carries a different promise to the public. We use it to help leaders decide, before engagement begins, how much influence the community will have over a given decision, and to design methods and communications that match that promise honestly.

faqs.q: How do you reach community members who do not usually participate?
faqs.a: We go where people already are rather than asking them to come to us. That means partnering with trusted community organizations, compensating participants for their time, offering childcare, food, translation and accessible formats, and scheduling around work and caregiving. We track who participates against who is affected so that gaps are visible during the process, not discovered afterward when it is too late to adjust.

faqs.q: Should community members be paid for participating in engagement?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. Residents who sit on advisory groups, co-design sessions or deliberative panels contribute expertise about their own lives and neighborhoods, often at personal cost. Compensation recognizes that expertise and makes participation possible for people who cannot donate unpaid time. We help clients set fair, consistent compensation policies that account for their procurement, tax and public benefits considerations.

faqs.q: What is the difference between community engagement and stakeholder engagement?
faqs.a: The terms overlap. Community engagement usually focuses on residents and local organizations affected by decisions in a particular place, with attention to equity and power. Stakeholder engagement is broader, covering investors, employees, regulators, suppliers, customers and advocacy groups, often across many places. Many clients need both, and we design them to complement each other rather than run as separate, competing processes.

services.name: Stakeholder Engagement
services.meta_description: Stakeholder engagement consulting: salience and impact mapping, materiality assessment and engagement routines that bring stakeholder insight into decisions.
services.summary: Identify the stakeholders who matter most to your strategy, understand what they need, and build engagement that strengthens trust and decisions.
services.lede: Our stakeholder engagement consulting helps leaders map who holds influence and who bears impact, understand their interests with evidence, and build engagement routines that inform strategy and earn durable trust.
challenge: Most organizations engage stakeholders reactively. Investor relations, government affairs, communications, HR and sustainability teams each maintain their own relationships, priorities and messages, with little coordination. When a controversy, regulatory change or major transaction arrives, leaders discover they do not have a clear view of who cares, what they care about or how much trust exists. Engagement becomes a defensive exercise in messaging rather than a source of insight that could have shaped the decision earlier.

There is also a structural blind spot. Stakeholders with power and urgency, such as large investors or regulators, get attention, while those who bear the greatest impact, such as frontline employees, suppliers' workers or nearby communities, are often consulted last or not at all. That imbalance creates risk, because overlooked groups can gain influence quickly, and it weakens decisions, because the people closest to the consequences often see problems first. Effective stakeholder engagement consulting corrects for both.

approach.title: Hearing stakeholders directly
approach.body: We conduct structured interviews and listening sessions across stakeholder groups, internal and external, to understand their interests, expectations, concerns and perceptions of your organization. Internal interviews with functional leaders reveal where relationships are held, what is already known and where messages to different audiences have drifted out of alignment over time.

approach.title: Mapping salience and materiality
approach.body: We build a stakeholder map using salience criteria of power, legitimacy and urgency, alongside an assessment of how significantly each group is affected by your decisions. Combined with a materiality assessment of the issues they raise, this shows where attention is concentrated, where it is missing and which issues carry both business and societal significance.

approach.title: Building an engagement architecture
approach.body: We design an engagement strategy that assigns each priority group an owner, a purpose, appropriate channels and a cadence, from information sharing to formal advisory panels. We set principles for consistency across functions, define escalation paths for emerging issues and build a mechanism for bringing stakeholder insight into leadership and board decision-making.

approach.title: Engaging and integrating insight
approach.body: We support launch of priority engagement activities, from investor and employee forums to multi-stakeholder roundtables, and coach executives who will lead them. Insights are synthesized and routed into the relevant decisions, such as strategy, product, capital allocation or policy positions, and stakeholders are told how their perspectives were considered.

approach.title: Tracking relationships over time
approach.body: We set up a shared stakeholder relationship register, trust and sentiment indicators, and a periodic materiality refresh. Governance assigns oversight to a named executive and, where appropriate, a board committee, so stakeholder engagement remains a managed discipline rather than an activity that fades when the immediate pressure passes.

deliverables: Stakeholder interview and listening synthesis report
Stakeholder map scored on power, legitimacy, urgency and impact
Materiality assessment of priority stakeholder issues
Engagement strategy with owners, channels and cadence
Executive briefing guides and advisory panel charters
Shared relationship register and trust indicator dashboard
outcomes: Leaders share an accurate, current view of who their key stakeholders are and what they expect.
Emerging issues are identified earlier, before they escalate into reputational or regulatory crises.
Groups most affected by decisions are heard alongside those with the most formal power.
Consistent messages and commitments across investor, employee, community and government relationships.
services.who_we_serve: We work with chief executives, chief sustainability and corporate affairs officers, investor relations and general counsel teams, and boards of companies, public institutions and large nonprofits. Trigger moments include preparing a first sustainability or double materiality assessment, entering a new market or community, a merger or restructuring that affects many groups, a public controversy, a new regulatory regime, or a board request for a clearer picture of stakeholder expectations and risks.
services.impact_lens: Stakeholder engagement done well distributes attention more fairly. Employees, suppliers' workers and communities who are affected by corporate decisions gain a channel to raise concerns before harm occurs. Customers and investors benefit from an organization that understands their expectations and keeps its commitments. And decisions informed by a wider range of perspectives tend to be more resilient, which supports long-term value for shareholders alongside the broader social good the organization affects.

faqs.q: What is stakeholder salience?
faqs.a: Stakeholder salience is a framework from management research that prioritizes stakeholders by three attributes: power to influence the organization, legitimacy of their relationship or claim, and urgency of their concerns. Groups holding more attributes typically receive more attention. We use salience alongside a separate assessment of how significantly each group is affected, because purely salience-based maps can overlook those who bear consequences but lack formal power.

faqs.q: How does stakeholder engagement support a materiality assessment?
faqs.a: A materiality assessment identifies which sustainability and business issues matter most, and stakeholder input is central to it. Under a double materiality approach, organizations assess both how issues affect enterprise value and how the organization affects people and the environment. Structured engagement provides the evidence for both perspectives and helps ensure the assessment reflects real stakeholder concerns rather than internal assumptions.

faqs.q: Who should own stakeholder engagement inside an organization?
faqs.a: Relationships will always be held by multiple functions, but someone must own the overall picture. We usually recommend a named executive accountable for coordination and insight, with functional owners for each priority group and periodic board oversight. The right structure depends on your size and sector; the key is that insights reach decision-makers and commitments are tracked across functions.

faqs.q: How do you measure the effectiveness of stakeholder engagement?
faqs.a: We combine relationship indicators with decision indicators. Relationship indicators include trust and sentiment measures, participation from priority groups and responsiveness to concerns. Decision indicators track whether stakeholder insight was considered in significant decisions and whether stakeholders were told how. Periodic qualitative check-ins with key groups provide context that numbers alone cannot, and help reveal emerging issues early.

services.name: Theory of Change Development
services.meta_title: Theory of Change Consulting and Logic Models
services.meta_description: Theory of change consulting that makes your causal logic explicit and testable: pathways, assumptions, logic models, indicators and a practical learning agenda.
services.summary: Make the causal logic of your work explicit, testable and shared, so strategy, measurement and funding decisions rest on clear assumptions.
services.lede: Our theory of change consulting helps organizations articulate how their activities lead to lasting outcomes, surface the assumptions that link each step, and turn that logic into a practical measurement and learning plan.
challenge: Funders, boards and government partners increasingly ask organizations to submit a theory of change, and many respond by producing a diagram for the proposal that is filed away once the grant is awarded. The diagram often lists activities on the left and aspirational impacts on the right, with arrows standing in for the hardest questions: why would this activity produce that change, for whom, under what conditions, and how would we know? Without those answers, measurement defaults to counting outputs and strategy discussions lack a common reference point.

Teams also disagree, often silently, about how change happens. Program staff, executives, evaluators and community partners carry different mental models built from different experiences. When those models are never surfaced, the organization pursues several implicit strategies at once, and evaluation findings are interpreted to suit each perspective. A useful theory of change brings those models into the open, reconciles them with evidence and with the lived experience of participants, and becomes a working tool rather than a compliance artifact.

approach.title: Surfacing how people believe change happens
approach.body: We interview staff, leadership, partners and program participants, asking each to describe how they believe the work creates change and what gets in the way. Participants' accounts are essential: they often reveal steps, barriers and outcomes that program designers miss, such as transportation, trust or caregiving constraints that determine whether an intervention reaches anyone.

approach.title: Testing the logic against evidence
approach.body: We review program data, prior evaluations and relevant research to assess the strength of each causal link. Assumptions are rated by how well evidence supports them and how critical they are to the overall logic, which identifies the few uncertain, high-stakes links that deserve priority attention in measurement, evaluation and program design.

approach.title: Building the theory and logic model
approach.body: In facilitated working sessions we work backward from long-term outcomes to define preconditions, then map the pathways, activities and outputs that contribute to them. The result is a narrative theory of change, a visual pathway diagram and a companion logic model, each stating assumptions, contextual factors and the boundary of what the organization contributes.

approach.title: Putting the theory to work
approach.body: We translate the theory into indicators for outputs, short-term and intermediate outcomes, select data sources and methods, and align program plans, grant proposals and staff roles with the pathways. Teams learn to use the theory when making design changes, so it guides decisions about what to start, adapt or stop.

approach.title: Learning and revising over time
approach.body: A theory of change should change as evidence accumulates. We set up a learning agenda with priority questions, a regular review where teams compare results to expectations, and a simple version history so updates are deliberate. Where useful, we prepare the ground for external evaluation by clarifying what can be credibly measured and attributed.

deliverables: Interviews on assumptions about how change happens
Evidence review and assumption strength assessment
Narrative theory of change and pathway diagram
Logic model linking activities, outputs and outcomes
Indicator framework and data collection plan
Learning agenda and evaluation readiness memo
outcomes: Staff, board and partners share a clear, common account of how the work creates change.
Measurement focuses on outcomes that matter, not only on activities and outputs.
Critical assumptions are identified and tested before major investments depend on them.
Funding proposals and evaluations rest on coherent, defensible logic that reviewers can follow.
services.who_we_serve: We work with nonprofit executive directors and program leaders, foundation program officers and evaluation staff, public agencies designing or commissioning programs, social enterprises and corporate impact teams. Common triggers include a funder requirement for a theory of change, preparation for an external evaluation, a strategic plan or program redesign, scaling a model to new sites, or a realization that staff and partners describe the organization's purpose and methods in noticeably different ways.
services.impact_lens: A rigorous theory of change protects the people programs are meant to serve. Participants' experiences shape the logic, so programs address the barriers they actually face. Staff gain clarity about how their daily work connects to outcomes, which supports motivation and better judgment. Funders and communities receive honest accounts of what an organization can and cannot achieve. And resources move toward approaches with stronger evidence, increasing the social good each dollar and hour can produce.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a theory of change and a logic model?
faqs.a: A theory of change explains why and how a set of activities is expected to produce long-term change, including the preconditions, causal pathways, assumptions and context involved. A logic model is usually a more linear, operational summary of inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes for a specific program. We typically develop both: the theory of change for strategy and learning, the logic model for management and reporting.

faqs.q: What is the difference between outputs and outcomes?
faqs.a: Outputs are the direct products of your activities, such as people trained, sessions delivered or grants made. Outcomes are the changes that result for people or conditions, such as new skills applied, employment obtained or health improved. Outputs are within your control and easy to count; outcomes are what actually matter to participants and funders, and they are where a theory of change should focus measurement.

faqs.q: How long does it take to develop a theory of change?
faqs.a: It depends on the complexity of the program and how many stakeholders need to be involved. A single, well-established program can move relatively quickly, while an organization-wide theory spanning several programs and partners requires more time for interviews, evidence review and consensus building. We prioritize participation over speed where the theory will guide significant decisions or investment.

faqs.q: Can a theory of change be used for evaluation?
faqs.a: Yes. A theory of change gives evaluators a framework to test whether each step in the expected pathway is occurring. Theory-based evaluation approaches, such as contribution analysis, use it to assess how plausibly a program contributed to observed outcomes, which is especially useful when randomized designs are impractical or inappropriate. We design theories with that future use in mind.

services.name: Nonprofit Strategy
services.meta_description: Nonprofit strategy consulting for boards and executives: strategic plans, program portfolio and true-cost analysis, revenue models and sustainable capacity.
services.summary: Strategic plans, business models and organizational capacity for nonprofits that need to grow impact without exhausting their people.
services.lede: Our nonprofit strategy consulting helps boards and executive teams make clear choices about mission, programs, revenue and organizational capacity, so the organization can deepen its impact while protecting the staff who deliver it.
challenge: Nonprofit leaders manage an unusual set of tensions. Restricted funding pulls programs in directions set by funders rather than by strategy. Growth often means adding programs faster than the infrastructure, systems and management capacity required to support them. Many organizations have a strategic plan that reads well but does not guide budgets or staffing, so year-to-year decisions are driven by grant deadlines. Boards want clarity on sustainability, while executives struggle to make the case for unrestricted investment in core operations.

The people cost is significant. Program staff take on expanding caseloads with modest pay, managers are promoted without preparation, and executive directors carry fundraising, operations and external relationships largely alone. Burnout and turnover erode institutional knowledge and relationships with the communities served. Nonprofit strategy consulting that ignores these conditions produces plans the organization cannot execute. Effective strategy treats staff capacity, equitable compensation and leadership depth as strategic choices, not as administrative afterthoughts.

approach.title: Hearing the whole organization
approach.body: We interview board members, executives, managers, frontline staff, funders and partners, and hold listening sessions with program participants where appropriate. A short all-staff survey captures views on mission clarity, workload and confidence in direction. The aim is to understand where the organization is genuinely effective, where it is stretched and what the community needs most.

approach.title: Assessing impact and economics together
approach.body: We analyze each program on two dimensions: contribution to mission, using available outcome evidence, and financial sustainability, using true cost including shared overhead. This matrix-based view, combined with a revenue mix analysis and a capacity assessment of leadership, systems and staffing, gives the board a clear, shared picture of strengths and pressures.

approach.title: Making the strategic choices
approach.body: With a strategy committee of board and staff, we set the intended impact, decide which programs to grow, sustain, redesign or transition, and define the revenue model and organizational investments that support those choices. Community members and frontline staff test options before they are finalized, so decisions reflect conditions on the ground.

approach.title: Turning the plan into operations
approach.body: We convert the strategy into an implementation roadmap, annual operating priorities, an aligned budget and a funder case for unrestricted or capacity-building support. Where structural changes are needed, such as new roles, a revised management layer or program transitions, we support planning, communication and change management with staff and partners.

approach.title: Governing for follow-through
approach.body: We help the board and executive team set a small number of strategic indicators, an operating dashboard and a quarterly review routine that links progress to budget decisions. Board committees receive clear roles in oversight, and staff leaders gain tools to update plans as conditions change without restarting the whole planning process.

deliverables: Stakeholder, staff and participant listening synthesis
Program portfolio analysis of mission impact and true cost
Organizational capacity and revenue model assessment
Board-approved strategic plan with intended impact statement
Implementation roadmap, aligned budget and funder case
Strategic dashboard and quarterly board review process
outcomes: A strategic plan that guides budget, staffing and program decisions, not just external messaging.
Programs aligned with mission and economics, with responsible transitions where change is needed.
A stronger case to funders for flexible, multiyear support of core operations.
Sustainable workloads and clearer leadership roles that reduce burnout and support staff retention.
services.who_we_serve: We work with nonprofit executive directors and chief executives, board chairs and strategy committees, chief operating officers and development leaders. Clients range from community-based organizations to national networks and affiliates. Common triggers include an expiring strategic plan, executive transition, rapid growth or the loss of a major funder, a merger or partnership opportunity, demand that has outpaced capacity, or a board seeking clearer evidence that programs are achieving the outcomes the organization promises.
services.impact_lens: A sound nonprofit strategy is ultimately about the people the organization serves. Clearer priorities mean programs can go deeper rather than wider, which typically improves quality for participants. Staff benefit from realistic workloads, defined roles and investment in leadership development. Funders gain confidence that their support is well used. And communities gain a more stable institution, one that can keep its commitments through funding cycles and leadership changes.

faqs.q: What does a nonprofit strategy consultant do?
faqs.a: A nonprofit strategy consultant helps leadership and the board clarify the organization's intended impact, assess programs, finances and capacity, and make choices about where to focus. The work typically includes stakeholder research, program and financial analysis, facilitated planning sessions and an implementation roadmap. Good consultants help the organization own the plan, building internal capacity to manage it rather than creating dependence.

faqs.q: How is a nonprofit strategic plan different from a business plan?
faqs.a: A business plan focuses on market opportunity, revenue and profitability. A nonprofit strategic plan starts with mission and intended impact, then addresses how programs, revenue, people and partnerships will advance it. Financial sustainability matters in both, but in a nonprofit it serves the mission. The best nonprofit plans integrate a clear business model, so leaders understand how each program is funded and what it truly costs.

faqs.q: Should our nonprofit consider a merger or strategic partnership?
faqs.a: Mergers, shared services and formal partnerships can increase impact and resilience when they are driven by mission rather than only by financial pressure. We help boards evaluate options by assessing mission alignment, cultural fit, service overlap, financial position and effects on staff and participants. In many cases, a less formal collaboration achieves the goal with lower risk. The analysis comes before the conversation with potential partners.

faqs.q: How do you involve staff and community in nonprofit strategic planning?
faqs.a: We use interviews, surveys and listening sessions to gather perspectives early, include frontline staff and community members on the planning committee or advisory group, and test draft options with them before decisions are final. Participants are compensated where appropriate. This produces a more grounded plan and builds the trust and understanding that implementation depends on.

services.name: Public Sector Consulting
services.meta_title: Public Sector Consulting for Government Agencies
services.meta_description: Public sector consulting that reduces administrative burden, strengthens the public workforce and helps agencies deliver policy goals with accountability.
services.summary: Help government agencies design services residents can use, build workforce capacity and deliver policy goals with accountability and evidence.
services.lede: Our public sector consulting helps government agencies improve resident-facing services, strengthen their workforce and operating models, and deliver policy priorities with the evidence, transparency and accountability that public institutions require.
challenge: Public agencies are asked to deliver more with constrained budgets, aging systems and a workforce facing significant retirement and recruitment pressures. New funding often arrives with tight timelines and complex compliance requirements. Residents compare government services with the best digital experiences they encounter elsewhere, yet agencies operate within statutes, procurement rules, legacy technology and multiple layers of oversight. The result is services that are difficult to navigate, especially for residents with limited time, language access, disabilities or digital connectivity.

Inside agencies, the people challenges are equally pressing. Hiring processes are slow, career pathways are unclear and frontline staff often absorb the friction of poorly designed processes. Policy teams, program staff, IT and procurement work in separate silos with different incentives. Change initiatives must survive election cycles and leadership transitions. Effective public sector consulting must respect these constraints, including civil service rules, collective bargaining and public records requirements, while still finding practical ways to improve service delivery.

approach.title: Understanding residents and public servants
approach.body: We conduct research with residents who use, or struggle to access, the service, including those most likely to be excluded. We also spend time with frontline staff, supervisors and partner organizations to understand how policy is actually implemented. This dual view reveals where statutory requirements end and where avoidable administrative burden begins, which is often surprisingly different.

approach.title: Establishing a service baseline
approach.body: We analyze administrative data on application volumes, processing times, error rates, approvals, denials and churn, disaggregated where lawful and appropriate to identify inequities. We map the service journey and calculate where time and effort concentrate for residents and staff, and assess workforce data on vacancies, turnover and capacity to see which constraints matter most.

approach.title: Co-designing feasible improvements
approach.body: We design changes with residents and staff, within legal and budget limits: simplified forms and notices, clearer eligibility communication, revised workflows, data sharing to reduce duplicate requests and role redesign. Where technology or services must be procured, we help define outcomes-based requirements and evaluation criteria that reflect the needs of the people using them.

approach.title: Implementing within public constraints
approach.body: We support pilots with clear success measures, then plan phased rollout, staff training, communications and labor-management engagement. We work alongside agency teams rather than in place of them, and we document decisions to support transparency, audit and public records requirements. Procurement and vendor management support helps keep implementation on schedule and accountable.

approach.title: Building lasting public capacity
approach.body: We help the agency establish service performance dashboards, regular review routines and a small internal team skilled in service design and data use. Playbooks and training materials ensure the approach survives leadership transitions, and public-facing reporting gives residents and elected officials a transparent view of progress toward the agency's goals.

Service journey map and administrative burden analysis
Equity-disaggregated service performance baseline report
Co-designed service improvements and pilot plans
Outcomes-based procurement requirements and evaluation criteria
Performance dashboard, playbooks and internal capability plan
outcomes: Residents can access services more easily, with less duplication, confusion and avoidable delay.
Frontline staff spend less time on rework and more time helping residents.
Procurements specify outcomes and user needs rather than only technical requirements.
Agency teams sustain improvements through leadership changes with their own skills and tools.
services.who_we_serve: We work with agency directors, deputy secretaries, chief operating and performance officers, program administrators and human resources leaders in city, county and state government, along with public authorities and quasi-governmental bodies. Typical triggers include new legislation or funding with implementation deadlines, persistent service backlogs, audit findings, workforce shortages, a modernization initiative, or a new administration seeking to translate policy priorities into measurable improvements for residents. We follow applicable procurement and conflict-of-interest requirements.
services.impact_lens: Public services shape whether people can access food, housing, health care, income and opportunity. Reducing administrative burden helps eligible residents receive the support intended for them, especially those with the least time and fewest resources to navigate complex systems. Public servants gain workflows that respect their expertise and reduce burnout. And taxpayers and elected officials gain clearer evidence of what public investment achieves, which strengthens trust in government institutions.

faqs.q: How do government agencies hire public sector consultants?
faqs.a: Agencies typically procure consulting services through competitive solicitations such as requests for proposals or qualifications, existing cooperative or statewide contracts, or, for smaller engagements, simplified procurement thresholds defined by their jurisdiction. Requirements vary by level of government and funding source. We work within the agency's procurement rules and can explain our approach to scope, deliverables and pricing in terms evaluators need.

faqs.q: What is administrative burden in public services?
faqs.a: Administrative burden refers to the learning, compliance and psychological costs people experience when interacting with government, such as figuring out eligibility, gathering documents, completing forms and dealing with stigma or uncertainty. Research in public administration shows these burdens can deter eligible people from receiving benefits. Reducing them through simpler processes, data sharing and clearer communication is a central aim of resident-centered service improvement.

faqs.q: Can human-centered design work within government regulations?
faqs.a: Yes. Statutes and regulations define what must happen, but agencies usually have considerable discretion over how: the wording of notices, the sequence of steps, which documents are requested and how staff are organized. Human-centered design focuses on that discretionary space. We work with legal and policy staff early to confirm what is required, so proposed changes are both resident-friendly and compliant.

faqs.q: How do you sustain improvements after leadership changes?
faqs.a: We build capability inside the agency rather than relying on consultants, document methods in playbooks, embed performance measures in routine management reviews and involve career staff throughout. Changes that are visible to residents and supported by frontline employees tend to have constituencies that outlast any single administration. Public reporting on progress also creates accountability that encourages continuity.

services.name: Corporate Social Responsibility
services.meta_description: Corporate social responsibility consulting that ties giving, volunteering and business practice to focused, measurable commitments that employees trust.
services.summary: Turn scattered CSR activity into a focused program tied to your business, your people and measurable community outcomes.
services.lede: Our corporate social responsibility consulting helps companies connect giving, volunteering, sourcing and business practices to a coherent strategy that employees believe in, communities value and stakeholders can verify.
challenge: Many corporate social responsibility programs are a collection of sponsorships, matching gifts, volunteer days and causes selected by different executives over many years. They generate goodwill but rarely produce measurable outcomes, and they are often disconnected from how the company actually affects people through its products, workforce, supply chain and footprint. As expectations from investors, regulators and employees rise, companies find that philanthropy alone no longer answers the question of whether the business itself is a responsible actor.

Employees notice the gap. Many want their employer to stand for something, yet they see CSR announcements that seem unrelated to their daily experience of pay, scheduling, safety or inclusion. Community partners notice when funding priorities shift with each leadership change. Communications teams worry about claims that cannot be substantiated. Corporate social responsibility consulting has to connect the external program with internal practice, so the company's commitments are consistent, credible and rooted in what the business does every day.

approach.title: Hearing employees and communities
approach.body: We gather perspectives from employees across levels and locations, community partners, customers and leaders through interviews, focus groups and short surveys. We ask how people experience the company's role in their lives and communities, what they value in current programs and where they see inconsistencies between stated commitments and actual business practice.

approach.title: Auditing the current footprint
approach.body: We inventory all current CSR activity, including giving, volunteering, in-kind support, sponsorships, supplier diversity and community investment, and map it against the company's most significant social impacts through operations, workforce and value chain. A peer and expectation scan identifies where your commitments trail stakeholder expectations or where your claims may be difficult to substantiate.

approach.title: Building a focused framework
approach.body: We help leadership choose a small number of focus areas where business capabilities, employee passion and community need intersect, and define how giving, volunteering, procurement and core practices will reinforce each other. Each focus area receives a theory of change, community partners selected through clear criteria and a governance model that survives executive turnover.

approach.title: Launching with employees
approach.body: We support the rollout of the refreshed program, including grant guidelines, skills-based volunteering design, employee resource group involvement, partner transitions handled with appropriate notice and internal communications. Managers receive talking points and tools so the program becomes part of how teams work, not an add-on announced once and then forgotten.

approach.title: Measuring and reporting credibly
approach.body: We develop outcome indicators for each focus area, simple partner reporting that does not burden small organizations, and an internal dashboard. Public reporting is aligned with relevant sustainability disclosure expectations and reviewed for substantiation, so the company can describe its contribution accurately and avoid overstated claims that damage trust.

deliverables: Employee and community partner listening synthesis
Inventory of CSR activity mapped to business impacts
Focus area framework with theory of change for each
Community partner selection criteria and transition plan
Skills-based volunteering and employee engagement program design
Outcome indicators, dashboard and reporting substantiation review
outcomes: A focused CSR program that reflects the company's real business impacts and capabilities.
Employees who understand, trust and participate in the company's community commitments.
Community partners with steadier, more predictable relationships and support from the company.
Public claims that can be substantiated and are consistent with internal business practice.
services.who_we_serve: We work with chief people officers, chief sustainability and corporate affairs officers, foundation and community investment leaders, and chief executives at companies of many sizes, including investor-backed businesses building their first program. Triggers include a new chief executive or brand repositioning, employee pressure for more meaningful engagement, a corporate foundation review, disclosure requirements, an acquisition that combines different programs, or recognition that current giving is diffuse and difficult to explain to employees and investors.
services.impact_lens: Responsible business starts inside the company. Aligning CSR with core practices means employees benefit from commitments that reach their own pay, safety, development and inclusion. Communities gain partners who stay committed and contribute skills as well as funding. Customers can trust that the company's claims reflect reality. And a CSR program built around genuine business strengths tends to deliver more social good per dollar while strengthening the company's reputation and ability to attract talent.

faqs.q: What is the difference between CSR and ESG?
faqs.a: Corporate social responsibility generally refers to a company's voluntary commitments to society, including philanthropy, volunteering and ethical practices. ESG refers to environmental, social and governance factors that investors and regulators use to assess risk, performance and disclosure. The two overlap substantially. A well-designed CSR strategy supports strong performance on the social dimension of ESG, while ESG frameworks add rigor to how CSR outcomes are measured and reported.

faqs.q: How do we choose CSR focus areas?
faqs.a: The strongest focus areas sit where three things meet: a significant community need, a distinctive company capability such as expertise, products or networks, and genuine employee interest. We also look at where the company's operations already affect people, positively or negatively, because commitments related to those impacts are more credible. Listening to employees and communities is essential before narrowing options.

faqs.q: What is skills-based volunteering?
faqs.a: Skills-based volunteering asks employees to contribute their professional expertise, such as finance, legal, technology, marketing or operations, to nonprofit and community partners. Done well, it addresses real capacity needs for partners and offers employees development opportunities. It requires careful scoping, partner input and time commitments that respect the partner's capacity to host volunteers, which is why we design it with partners rather than for them.

faqs.q: How do we avoid greenwashing or impact-washing in CSR reporting?
faqs.a: Report outcomes alongside activities, describe contribution rather than claiming sole credit, disclose limitations and setbacks, and keep evidence on file for every public claim. Reporting should also cover the company's material negative impacts, not only its positive programs. We conduct a substantiation review of claims before publication and align reporting with relevant disclosure standards and advertising guidance.

services.name: Workforce Development Programs
services.meta_description: Workforce development consulting for employers, workforce boards and funders: sector partnerships, career pathways and outcomes measured by quality jobs.
services.summary: Design employer-led training and career pathways that connect people to quality jobs and give employers the skilled talent they need.
services.lede: Our workforce development consulting helps employers, intermediaries, public workforce boards and funders design sector partnerships and career pathway programs that lead to quality jobs, measured by advancement and retention, not only enrollment.
challenge: Employers report persistent difficulty filling skilled roles, while many workers remain in low-wage jobs with few routes to advancement. Workforce programs exist to close that gap, but many are designed from the supply side: a training provider builds a curriculum, enrolls participants and hopes employers will hire graduates. Without employer commitment to hiring, aligned credentials and realistic job quality, graduates struggle to find work that uses their new skills, and employers continue to see programs as disconnected from their needs.

The people barriers are equally real. Participants juggle training with work, caregiving, transportation and financial pressure, and many drop out for reasons that have nothing to do with ability. Employers' hiring practices may screen out qualified candidates through degree requirements or rigid scheduling. Supervisors may be unprepared to support new hires. Effective workforce development consulting addresses the full system: employer demand, training design, wraparound supports, hiring practices and the job quality that determines whether people stay and advance.

approach.title: Understanding employers and job seekers
approach.body: We interview employers about specific skill needs, hiring practices and retention challenges, and conduct research with current and prospective participants about their goals and barriers. Conversations with training providers, community organizations and workforce boards reveal the existing ecosystem, where referrals break down and which supports participants rely on to complete training and keep their jobs.

approach.title: Analyzing demand, outcomes and job quality
approach.body: We analyze labor market data for target occupations, assess wages, benefits, scheduling and advancement potential, and review existing program data on enrollment, completion, placement, retention and earnings, disaggregated to reveal equity gaps. A skills analysis compares what employers require with what current credentials and curricula actually teach.

approach.title: Building the sector partnership and pathway
approach.body: We co-design an employer-led sector partnership with a shared governance model, then design career pathways with stackable credentials, work-based learning such as apprenticeships, and wraparound supports for transportation, childcare and income. Employers commit to skills-based hiring, supervisor preparation and clear advancement steps, so training leads to quality jobs and progression.

approach.title: Launching and supporting implementation
approach.body: We support the launch of pilot cohorts, employer onboarding, partner agreements, data sharing arrangements and participant recruitment through trusted community channels. Supervisors and mentors receive training to support new hires. We also help prepare funding proposals and braided funding plans that combine public workforce, philanthropic and employer resources to sustain the program.

approach.title: Tracking outcomes and improving
approach.body: We establish shared outcome measures across partners, focused on placement, retention, wage growth and advancement, with dashboards that inform regular partnership meetings. Participant feedback loops identify barriers early. A continuous improvement process helps the partnership adapt curricula and supports as employer needs change and evidence accumulates about which elements work.

Participant barrier research and support needs assessment
Sector partnership charter and governance model
Career pathway map with stackable credentials and work-based learning
Braided funding plan and employer commitment agreements
Shared outcome measures and partnership performance dashboard
outcomes: Training aligned with real employer demand, leading to quality jobs rather than certificates alone.
Higher completion as participants receive the supports they need to finish training.
Employers adopt skills-based hiring and supervisor practices that improve new hire retention.
A durable partnership that can sustain funding and adapt to changing labor market needs.
services.who_we_serve: We work with employer human resources and talent acquisition leaders, workforce development boards, community colleges, training intermediaries, economic development agencies and foundations that fund economic mobility. Engagements often begin with a new public or philanthropic funding opportunity, an employer facing persistent hiring shortages, a regional economic development project, a program with strong enrollment but weak placement or retention outcomes, or a coalition seeking to formalize an informal partnership into a governed sector strategy.
services.impact_lens: Effective workforce development changes lives and local economies. Participants gain skills, credentials and access to jobs with better wages, benefits and advancement potential. Employers gain a pipeline of prepared workers and supervisors who can retain them. Communities benefit from greater economic mobility and reduced barriers for residents who have been excluded from good jobs. And because programs are designed with employers and participants, public and philanthropic investment is more likely to produce lasting results.

faqs.q: What is a sector partnership in workforce development?
faqs.a: A sector partnership brings multiple employers within an industry together with training providers, workforce boards, community organizations and sometimes labor organizations to address shared talent needs. Employers lead in defining skills and committing to hiring, while partners coordinate training, recruitment and support services. Sector strategies are widely regarded in workforce research as one of the more promising approaches for improving both earnings and employer outcomes.

faqs.q: How do you measure the success of a workforce development program?
faqs.a: We focus on outcomes rather than outputs. Enrollment and completion matter, but the critical measures are placement in quality jobs, retention over time, wage growth and advancement. We disaggregate results by demographic group to reveal equity gaps, combine program data with employer and participant feedback, and track job quality indicators such as benefits and scheduling stability.

faqs.q: What is skills-based hiring?
faqs.a: Skills-based hiring evaluates candidates on demonstrated abilities rather than proxies such as degrees or years of experience. It can widen talent pools and improve equity, but it requires redesigning job descriptions, assessments and interview processes, and training hiring managers to apply them consistently. We help employers identify which roles are suitable and build the practices that make skills-based hiring work in practice, not only in policy.

faqs.q: How are workforce development programs funded?
faqs.a: Most successful programs braid several funding sources: public workforce funds, education and apprenticeship funding, philanthropic grants and employer contributions such as wages during training, equipment, instructors or tuition support. Each source carries different eligibility and reporting requirements. We help partnerships design a funding plan that covers core coordination costs, avoids dependence on any single source and aligns reporting across funders.

services.name: Philanthropy Advisory
services.meta_description: Philanthropy advisory for foundations, families and corporate funders: grantmaking strategy, trust-based practice, grantee feedback and learning that lasts.
services.summary: Advise foundations, families and corporate funders on grantmaking strategy, trust-based practice and learning that helps grantees and communities thrive.
services.lede: Our philanthropy advisory helps foundations, family offices, donor-advised fund holders and corporate funders clarify their goals, design grantmaking strategies and practices that respect grantees, and learn from their giving over time.
challenge: Philanthropic resources are significant, but strategies are often shaped by founders' early interests, board preferences or the accumulation of legacy grants. Funders may spread grants thinly across many issues, impose application and reporting requirements out of proportion to grant size, or change priorities abruptly. Families face additional complexity when generations hold different values, while corporate foundations balance community goals with business expectations. Without clarity of purpose and approach, philanthropy can produce goodwill without the sustained change donors hope to achieve.

Power dynamics shape every grantmaking relationship. Grantees often feel unable to speak candidly about challenges for fear of losing funding, so funders receive optimistic reports rather than useful information. Restricted, short-term grants make it difficult for nonprofits to invest in staff, systems and resilience. Communities affected by funding decisions are rarely involved in making them. Thoughtful philanthropy advisory addresses not only what to fund but how to fund: the practices, relationships and accountability that determine whether giving strengthens or strains the field.

approach.title: Clarifying values and hearing grantees
approach.body: We interview trustees, family members, staff and leaders to clarify values, goals, time horizon and appetite for risk. We also gather candid feedback from current and former grantees, through anonymous surveys and third-party interviews, and from community leaders, so the strategy reflects how the funder's practices are actually experienced in the field.

approach.title: Reviewing the grant portfolio
approach.body: We analyze the grant portfolio by issue, geography, grant size, duration, restriction and grantee characteristics, and assess what is known about results. We compare the funder's application, reporting and payment practices against its grant sizes, and estimate the burden placed on grantees, which often reveals easy opportunities to reduce friction and redirect staff time to relationships.

approach.title: Designing strategy and practice
approach.body: We help the board choose focus areas, a theory of change for each and a grantmaking approach: general operating or project support, multiyear commitments, capacity building, participatory grantmaking, program-related investments or policy engagement. We also design grant practices consistent with trust-based philanthropy principles, such as streamlined applications, flexible funding and reporting that serves learning.

approach.title: Transitioning and launching
approach.body: We support the transition from current to future portfolio, including responsible exit plans with adequate notice and tapering for grantees who fall outside new priorities. We help revise guidelines, update grants management workflows, design community advisory structures where appropriate and prepare staff and trustees for new roles in relationship-based grantmaking.

approach.title: Learning and accountability
approach.body: We set up a learning framework that combines grantee feedback, outcome evidence and periodic strategy reviews, with indicators the board can track without imposing new reporting on grantees. Regular grantee perception feedback holds the funder accountable for its own practices, and a cycle of review allows strategy to evolve as conditions and evidence change.
