Anonymous grantee perception feedback and analysis
Grant portfolio analysis by focus, size and flexibility
Grantmaking strategy with theory of change per focus area
Revised grant practices, guidelines and responsible exit plan
Learning framework and board strategy review process
outcomes: A grantmaking strategy that reflects donors' values and the priorities of affected communities.
Grantees spend less time on applications and reports and more on their mission.
Funders receive candid information that improves decisions and strengthens grantee relationships.
Trustees and staff share a clear framework for evaluating progress and adapting strategy.
services.who_we_serve: We advise foundation chief executives and boards, family foundations and family offices, donor-advised fund holders with significant giving, corporate foundations and community foundations. Typical triggers include a generational transition in a family foundation, a significant new gift or liquidity event, a new foundation president, a decision to spend down or extend the foundation's life, grantee feedback revealing problematic practices, or a board desire to concentrate resources for greater impact and better learning.
services.impact_lens: Philanthropic practices shape the health of the nonprofit sector and the communities it serves. Flexible, multiyear funding lets grantees invest in staff, fair compensation and resilience. Streamlined processes return time to mission delivery. Including community voices in grantmaking shifts some decision-making power to the people most affected. And funders who learn honestly from grantees make better decisions, so each philanthropic dollar contributes more fully to lasting social good.

faqs.q: What is trust-based philanthropy?
faqs.a: Trust-based philanthropy is an approach to grantmaking that seeks to address power imbalances between funders and grantees. Its commonly cited practices include providing multiyear unrestricted funding, doing the homework so grantees do not have to, simplifying paperwork, being transparent and responsive, soliciting and acting on feedback, and offering support beyond the check. It does not mean abandoning accountability; it means building accountability through relationships and learning.

faqs.q: Should a foundation provide general operating support or project grants?
faqs.a: General operating support gives grantees flexibility to invest where they see the greatest need, including staff, systems and reserves, and is generally more aligned with nonprofit sustainability. Project grants can suit time-limited initiatives or new programs with clear boundaries. Many funders use a mix. The right balance depends on the funder's goals, relationships and confidence in grantees' leadership and strategy.

faqs.q: What is participatory grantmaking?
faqs.a: Participatory grantmaking shifts some or all funding decisions to people affected by the issues being funded, such as community residents, people with lived experience or grantee peers. Models range from community advisory committees that inform staff recommendations to panels that make final decisions. It requires careful design around eligibility, compensation, conflicts of interest and support, but it can improve both decisions and legitimacy.

faqs.q: How can a family foundation manage different generations' priorities?
faqs.a: We start by listening to each generation separately and together, identifying shared values and areas of difference. Options include a shared core strategy with discretionary grants for individual family members, next-generation committees, or distinct focus areas led by different branches. Clear governance, documented donor intent where relevant and facilitated decision-making help families sustain both the foundation and their relationships.

services.name: Strategic Planning
services.meta_description: Strategic planning consulting that forces real trade-offs, involves the people who execute the plan, and builds the routines that keep strategy alive all year.
services.summary: Set clear direction, make real trade-offs and build the management routines that turn a strategic plan into daily decisions.
services.lede: Our strategic planning consulting helps leadership teams and boards make explicit choices about where to compete or serve, how to win, and what to stop, then translate those choices into priorities managers can act on.
challenge: Strategic plans often fail in one of two ways. Some are so broad that every existing initiative fits inside them, so nothing changes. Others are thoughtful but disconnected from budgeting, staffing and performance management, so they are revisited once a year and ignored in between. In both cases leaders have not made the hard choices about what the organization will not do, and managers are left to interpret competing priorities on their own, often by defaulting to the most urgent request.

Planning processes also tend to exclude the people who know the most about customers and operations. Strategy is written by a small group, communicated in a town hall and then cascaded as a list of targets. Middle managers, who must translate strategy into team decisions, receive little context about why choices were made. Employees cannot see how their work connects to the plan. Strategic planning consulting should produce a plan with genuine choices and a process that builds understanding and commitment across the organization.

approach.title: Gathering perspectives across the organization
approach.body: We interview the board and leadership team, hold structured conversations with managers and frontline employees, and gather customer, partner and investor perspectives. An organization-wide survey captures views on current direction, priorities and barriers to execution. This research often reveals disagreement among leaders that must be addressed before any plan can work in practice.

approach.title: Establishing a strategic fact base
approach.body: We build a fact base on market dynamics, customer needs, competitive or peer position, financial performance and organizational capabilities, including people metrics such as engagement, turnover and capability gaps. Scenario analysis tests how different futures would affect the organization, so the plan is robust to uncertainty rather than dependent on a single forecast.

approach.title: Making explicit choices
approach.body: In facilitated sessions, leadership defines its aspiration, where to play, how to win, the capabilities required and the management systems that support them. Options are evaluated against the fact base and tested with managers and employees. We insist on explicit trade-offs: what will receive more investment, what will receive less and what will stop entirely.

approach.title: Translating strategy into action
approach.body: We convert choices into a small set of strategic priorities, objectives and key results, initiative charters with owners and resource requirements, and an aligned budget. Managers receive briefing materials and facilitation guides to discuss the strategy with their teams and translate it into team-level goals, so the plan reaches the front line.

approach.title: Governing execution
approach.body: We design a strategy management routine: quarterly strategy reviews held separately from operational meetings, a dashboard of leading and lagging indicators, and a process for adjusting priorities when assumptions change. Board reporting focuses on progress against strategic choices. We build internal capability so the organization can run future planning cycles itself.

deliverables: Leadership, employee and stakeholder perspectives synthesis
Strategic fact base and scenario analysis
Strategy on a page with explicit trade-offs
Objectives and key results with initiative charters
Manager briefing kit and team cascade guides
Strategy dashboard and quarterly review operating rhythm
outcomes: A leadership team aligned on clear choices, including what the organization will stop doing.
Budgets, staffing and initiatives that reflect strategic priorities rather than historical patterns.
Managers and employees who understand the strategy and can connect it to their work.
A governance rhythm that keeps the plan current as conditions and evidence change.
services.who_we_serve: We work with chief executives, chief strategy officers, executive teams and boards in companies, investor-backed businesses, nonprofits, health systems, universities and public institutions. Common triggers include a new chief executive or board chair, the end of a planning cycle, a significant market shift, an ownership change or new investment, a merger, underperformance against plan, or a recognition that the current strategy is not shaping decisions because it lacks clear priorities and trade-offs.
services.impact_lens: A clear strategy is a gift to the people who carry it out. Employees spend less effort on conflicting priorities and initiatives that will never be funded. Managers can make decisions with confidence. Customers experience a more consistent organization. When planning includes community and stakeholder perspectives, the plan is more likely to account for the organization's broader effects. And focused resource allocation strengthens the financial performance that sustains jobs and investment over time.

faqs.q: What does a strategic planning consultant do?
faqs.a: A strategic planning consultant designs and facilitates the planning process, builds the fact base, challenges assumptions and helps leaders make and document clear choices. They also help translate strategy into priorities, budgets and governance routines. An effective consultant brings outside perspective and analytical rigor while ensuring the leadership team owns the strategy and has the capability to manage it after the engagement ends.

faqs.q: How many years should a strategic plan cover?
faqs.a: Many organizations plan over a multiyear horizon with annual operating priorities and quarterly reviews. The right horizon depends on how quickly your industry or environment changes and how long major investments take to mature. More important than the horizon is the review rhythm: a plan revisited quarterly and adjusted as evidence emerges is more useful than a longer plan left unchanged.

faqs.q: How do you involve employees in strategic planning without slowing it down?
faqs.a: We gather employee input early through surveys, focus groups and manager conversations, so it shapes the fact base rather than arriving late. We test draft choices with representative groups and use their feedback to refine implementation. Leadership retains decision rights, but employees understand the reasoning. This adds little time and typically accelerates execution because fewer people need to be persuaded later.

faqs.q: What is the difference between strategic planning and operational planning?
faqs.a: Strategic planning decides direction: where the organization will focus, how it will create value and which capabilities it needs. Operational planning determines how work will be organized, resourced and scheduled to deliver those choices in a given period. Both are necessary. Problems arise when operational plans are built without reference to strategy, or when strategy is set without regard to operational capacity.

services.name: Operating Model Design
services.meta_description: Operating model design that aligns capabilities, structure, decision rights, processes and technology with strategy, and guides the people transition carefully.
services.summary: Redesign how work, decisions, people and technology fit together so your organization can deliver its strategy reliably and at scale.
services.lede: Our operating model design work helps leaders define how value is delivered: the capabilities, structures, decision rights, processes, technology and people practices required to execute strategy without unnecessary complexity.
challenge: Operating models usually evolve by accumulation. Functions add teams, regions add local processes, acquisitions bring parallel systems, and shared services are created without clear service levels. Over time the organization becomes harder to navigate: decisions require too many approvals, accountabilities overlap, and customers experience inconsistency depending on which part of the organization they encounter. Leaders sense that cost and speed are suffering but struggle to pinpoint where, because the operating model has never been described as a whole.

Redesign efforts often fail by focusing on structure alone. A new organization chart is announced, yet decision rights, governance forums, processes, metrics and incentives remain unchanged, so work continues much as before under different names. Employees experience uncertainty and lost relationships without seeing improvement. Effective operating model design treats structure as one element among several and pays attention to how people will actually work, decide and collaborate under the new design, including the managers who must make it function.

approach.title: Understanding how work really happens
approach.body: We interview leaders and conduct workshops with managers and frontline staff to understand where decisions get stuck, where handoffs fail and where work is duplicated. Customer and employee perspectives reveal how the current model is experienced, which is often different from how it is described in organization charts and policy documents.

approach.title: Diagnosing the current model
approach.body: We build a current-state view using an operating model canvas covering value chain, capabilities, organization, locations, information systems, suppliers and management system. Activity analysis, spans and layers analysis, decision-rights mapping and cost-to-serve data show where complexity, cost and delay concentrate, establishing a baseline for evaluating design options.

approach.title: Designing options with clear principles
approach.body: With leadership, we set design principles derived from strategy, then develop and evaluate alternative models: centralized, decentralized, hybrid, platform or shared services. The preferred design specifies capabilities, structure, decision rights using tools such as RAPID or RACI, governance forums, key processes, roles and metrics. Managers and employees test the design through realistic scenarios.

approach.title: Transitioning with care
approach.body: We develop a transition plan covering sequencing, role mapping, talent selection, consultation obligations, communications and change management. Leaders and managers receive guidance on holding individual conversations with affected employees. Implementation proceeds in waves with readiness checks, so business continuity is protected and issues are resolved before the next phase begins.

approach.title: Embedding the new model
approach.body: After transition, we track adoption and performance indicators, run pulse surveys to understand the employee experience of the change and conduct post-implementation reviews. Governance forums are calibrated, decision rights are reinforced and adjustments are made where the design is not working, so the operating model continues to evolve with strategy rather than ossifying again.

deliverables: Current-state operating model canvas and diagnostic
Spans, layers and decision-rights analysis
Design principles and evaluated operating model options
Target operating model with roles, governance and metrics
Transition roadmap, role mapping and change plan
Adoption dashboard and post-implementation review findings
outcomes: Clear accountabilities and decision rights that reduce delays, duplication and unnecessary escalation.
An organization structured around the capabilities that matter most to the strategy.
Customers experience greater consistency across channels, regions and business units.
Employees and managers understand their roles and how work flows across the organization.
services.who_we_serve: We work with chief executives, chief operating officers, chief people officers and transformation leaders in companies, portfolio companies, health systems, nonprofits and public agencies. Engagements are often triggered by a new strategy, rapid growth that has outpaced the existing structure, an acquisition or merger, a move to shared services, a cost or efficiency mandate, a shift to digital or AI-enabled delivery, or persistent complaints that the organization has become slow and difficult to navigate.
services.impact_lens: Operating models determine the daily working lives of employees and the experience customers receive. A well-designed model gives people clear roles, reasonable spans of control and the authority to make decisions close to the work. Customers benefit from simpler, more reliable service. Transitions handled with transparency and fairness protect trust. And an efficient model frees resources for investment in people, products and the communities the organization serves.

faqs.q: What is an operating model?
faqs.a: An operating model describes how an organization delivers value to customers or beneficiaries. It covers the capabilities required, how work is organized into structures and processes, who makes which decisions, the technology and data that support the work, where work is done, the partners involved and the management system of metrics and governance. It translates strategy into the day-to-day mechanics of the organization.

faqs.q: What is an operating model canvas?
faqs.a: The operating model canvas is a one-page tool, developed by Andrew Campbell and colleagues, for describing an operating model across elements such as value delivery chains, organization, locations, information, suppliers and management system. We use it to create a shared picture of the current and target model, making it easier for leaders to compare options and see how changes in one element affect others.

faqs.q: How is operating model design different from a restructuring?
faqs.a: A restructuring typically changes reporting lines and roles, often with a cost objective. Operating model design is broader: it considers capabilities, processes, decision rights, governance, technology and metrics as well as structure. A restructuring may be one outcome, but without changes to how decisions are made and how work flows, structural changes alone rarely deliver the intended improvement.

faqs.q: How do you minimize disruption to employees during operating model change?
faqs.a: We involve managers and employees in testing the design, communicate clearly about what is known and unknown, and follow fair, consistent processes for role mapping and selection. Transitions are phased with readiness checks. Managers receive training for difficult conversations, and pulse surveys help leaders respond to concerns quickly. Change is never painless, but transparency and fairness strongly affect how it is experienced.

services.name: Process Improvement
services.meta_description: Process improvement consulting using lean methods, value stream mapping and frontline co-design to cut delay and rework while making work simpler for people.
services.summary: Use lean methods and frontline insight to remove waste, reduce errors and give people more time for the work that matters.
services.lede: Our process improvement consulting combines lean methods, value stream mapping and frontline co-design to reduce delay, rework and cost, while making work simpler for the employees who do it and the customers it serves.
challenge: Most organizations carry processes that grew by exception. A control was added after an error, an approval was inserted after a dispute, a workaround became standard practice when a system could not handle a common case. Each change made sense at the time, but together they create long lead times, multiple handoffs and high rework. Customers wait, costs rise and capacity is consumed by checking, chasing and correcting rather than by the work customers actually value.

Employees experience this as frustration. They spend time hunting for information, re-entering data across systems and resolving problems created upstream, often without authority to fix the root cause. Improvement programs that are imposed from above, focused on headcount reduction or driven by consultants who do not understand the work can deepen cynicism. Effective process improvement consulting engages the people closest to the work, focuses on flow and quality and treats freed capacity as something to redeploy thoughtfully.

approach.title: Going to where the work happens
approach.body: We observe work directly, following requests, cases or products through the process, and interview the employees who perform each step. Customers or internal clients describe their experience and what they value. This gemba-style observation reveals the workarounds, waiting and informal knowledge that never appear in process documentation or system reports.

approach.title: Mapping the value stream
approach.body: We build current-state value stream maps showing each step, handoff, wait time and rework loop, and calculate lead time, process time, first-pass yield and demand patterns. Failure demand, meaning work caused by earlier errors or unclear communication, is quantified. This baseline distinguishes value-adding work from waste and highlights the constraints that limit flow.

approach.title: Co-designing the future state
approach.body: In improvement workshops, cross-functional teams design a future-state process: eliminating unnecessary steps, reducing handoffs, standardizing work where variation causes errors, and redesigning roles and decision rights so issues are resolved at first contact. Automation is considered after the process is simplified, so technology does not encode existing waste.

approach.title: Piloting and implementing
approach.body: We run rapid improvement cycles using plan-do-study-act methods, testing changes in a pilot area before broader rollout. Updated standard work, training, visual management boards and job aids support adoption. Where capacity is released, we work with leaders to redeploy it toward customer-facing, higher-value or backlog work, with clear and honest communication to employees.

approach.title: Building a continuous improvement culture
approach.body: We establish daily or weekly huddles, process performance metrics and tiered escalation, and train internal improvement leads and managers in lean problem-solving. Process owners are named and accountable for performance. This builds a sustainable improvement system in which employees identify and solve problems routinely, rather than depending on periodic external projects.

deliverables: Direct observation findings and employee interview synthesis
Current-state value stream maps with lead time analysis
Failure demand and rework quantification
Co-designed future-state process and standard work
Pilot results, rollout plan and capacity redeployment plan
Tiered huddle system, metrics and improvement training
outcomes: Shorter lead times and fewer errors for customers and internal clients alike.
Employees spend less time on rework, chasing information and duplicate data entry.
Process owners with clear accountability and the data to manage performance.
A continuous improvement habit that persists after the initial project concludes.
services.who_we_serve: We work with chief operating officers, operations and shared services leaders, quality and continuous improvement leaders, and portfolio company operating partners in healthcare, financial services, manufacturing, public agencies and professional services. Engagements often follow customer complaints about delays, growing backlogs, margin pressure, a systems implementation that requires process redesign, an acquisition integrating different processes, or employee feedback indicating that broken processes are a major driver of frustration and turnover.
services.impact_lens: Process improvement affects people on both sides of a transaction. Customers receive faster, more reliable service with fewer errors. Employees gain workflows that respect their time and expertise, and a voice in how work is designed. When improvement is used to redeploy capacity rather than only to cut cost, organizations can expand services, reduce burnout and invest in growth, creating value for employees, customers and communities that extends beyond the financial results.

faqs.q: What is value stream mapping?
faqs.a: Value stream mapping is a lean technique for visualizing every step required to deliver a product or service, from request to completion, including the flow of information and materials. It records process times, wait times, handoffs and rework, distinguishing value-adding activity from waste. Teams use the current-state map to identify problems and design a future-state map that improves flow.

faqs.q: What is the difference between lean and Six Sigma?
faqs.a: Lean focuses on improving flow and eliminating waste, such as waiting, rework, unnecessary movement and overprocessing. Six Sigma focuses on reducing variation and defects using statistical methods. Many organizations combine them. We select methods based on the problem: lean for flow and handoff issues, statistical analysis where variation and quality defects are the main concern, and service design methods where customer experience is central.

faqs.q: Will process improvement lead to job cuts?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, and we recommend that leaders decide and communicate their intentions early. Many organizations redeploy released capacity to backlogs, growth, customer service or new capabilities. Where workforce reductions are being considered, honesty matters, because employees will not share improvement ideas if they believe doing so threatens their colleagues. Clear commitments about how capacity will be used are essential to engagement.

faqs.q: Should we automate processes before or after improving them?
faqs.a: Generally after. Automating a poorly designed process can make waste faster and harder to change. We first simplify and standardize the process, remove unnecessary steps and clarify decision rules. Then we identify which remaining steps are well suited to automation or AI support, and design how employees will work alongside those tools, including exception handling and oversight.

services.name: Mission-Driven Growth Strategy
services.meta_description: Mission-driven growth strategy for social enterprises, B Corps and mission-led companies: scale revenue and impact together without drifting from your purpose.
services.summary: Grow revenue, reach and impact together, with growth strategies that strengthen rather than dilute your mission and stakeholder trust.
services.lede: Our mission-driven growth strategy work helps social enterprises, B Corps, mission-led companies and earned-revenue nonprofits find growth paths where commercial success and social impact reinforce each other, and protect the mission as they scale.
challenge: Mission-driven organizations face distinctive growth challenges. Investors and lenders expect growth, yet some paths to scale, such as moving upmarket, entering new channels or cutting costs in the supply chain, can pull the organization away from the people it was founded to serve. Leaders may not have a framework for evaluating whether a growth opportunity strengthens or weakens the mission, so decisions depend on individual instinct or are deferred until a crisis forces a choice.

Growth also strains culture and people. Early employees who joined for the mission may feel that new hires, processes or investors are changing the organization's character. Founders struggle to delegate. Impact measurement that worked at small scale breaks down. Customers and community partners notice when service quality slips or priorities shift. Mission-driven growth strategy must address the economics of scale as well as the governance, culture and accountability mechanisms that keep the mission central as the organization grows.

approach.title: Understanding mission and market
approach.body: We interview founders, leaders, board members, investors, employees and customers, and conduct research with the communities the organization serves. We seek to understand what the mission means in practice, which customers or beneficiaries are core, and where stakeholders see risks of mission drift, as well as what customers value and where unmet demand exists.

approach.title: Analyzing impact and economics together
approach.body: We analyze unit economics, customer segments, channel performance and market size alongside impact data, assessing how each segment and offering contributes to both revenue and mission outcomes. An impact-economics matrix shows which activities are self-sustaining, which require subsidy and which generate surplus that can fund mission work, informing realistic choices about growth.

approach.title: Selecting growth paths
approach.body: We develop and evaluate growth options, such as new segments, products, geographies, partnerships, licensing, franchising or acquisitions, against both financial and impact criteria. Mission guardrails define what the organization will not compromise. Customers and community members test concepts, and the strategy specifies the capital requirements and investor fit needed to pursue the chosen path.

approach.title: Scaling with integrity
approach.body: We support implementation of priority growth initiatives, including go-to-market planning, partnership agreements, organization design and talent strategy for scaling. We help founders and leaders adapt their roles, design onboarding that conveys mission and culture to new employees, and prepare investor and board communications about how growth and impact goals will be managed together.

approach.title: Governing mission and growth together
approach.body: We help establish integrated performance dashboards that track impact alongside financial metrics, governance mechanisms such as mission committees or legal structures that protect purpose, and regular reviews that test whether growth is advancing the mission. These mechanisms help preserve the organization's purpose through future funding rounds, leadership changes or ownership transitions.

deliverables: Stakeholder and customer research on mission and value
Impact-economics matrix by segment, product and channel
Evaluated growth options with explicit mission guardrails
Growth strategy with capital requirements and investor fit
Scaling plan for organization, talent and culture
Integrated impact and financial performance dashboard
outcomes: Growth decisions evaluated consistently against both financial performance and mission outcomes.
Clear guardrails that help leaders recognize and avoid mission drift as they scale.
Investors, lenders and board members aligned on how growth and impact will be balanced.
A culture and governance structure that carry the mission through scale and transitions.
services.who_we_serve: We work with founders and chief executives of social enterprises, B Corps and benefit corporations, mission-driven consumer and technology companies, earned-revenue nonprofits, community development financial institutions, and their boards and investors. Typical triggers include preparing for a funding round, considering a new market or acquisition, a plateau after early growth, investor pressure to scale faster, founder transition, or concern among employees and customers that the organization is drifting from its original purpose.
services.impact_lens: When growth and mission reinforce each other, scale means more people served, not only more revenue. Customers and beneficiaries gain wider access to products and services designed with their needs in mind. Employees keep the sense of purpose that drew them to the organization. Communities benefit from enterprises that remain accountable as they grow. And investors gain businesses whose mission strengthens customer loyalty, talent attraction and resilience, supporting long-term financial returns.

faqs.q: What is mission drift and how can growing organizations prevent it?
faqs.a: Mission drift occurs when an organization gradually moves away from its core purpose, often because commercial pressures, funding requirements or growth opportunities pull activity toward more profitable or easier-to-serve segments. Prevention requires explicit mission guardrails, impact metrics reviewed alongside financial metrics, governance that holds leadership accountable for both, and investors whose expectations are aligned with the mission from the start.

faqs.q: How do social enterprises balance profit and purpose?
faqs.a: The most durable social enterprises design business models where impact is integral to value creation, so serving the mission and generating revenue rely on the same activities. Where the two diverge, they make deliberate choices, such as cross-subsidizing mission work with profitable segments or seeking blended capital. Clarity about which activities sustain the organization and which require subsidy is essential to managing the balance.

faqs.q: Does B Corp certification or benefit corporation status help protect mission during growth?
faqs.a: They can help. Benefit corporation status, where available, embeds stakeholder consideration in a company's legal duties, and B Corp certification provides an external standard and assessment. Neither substitutes for strategy, culture and governance, but both can reinforce mission commitments with investors, acquirers and employees. We help leaders evaluate whether these structures fit their circumstances, alongside advice from legal counsel.

faqs.q: What kinds of capital suit mission-driven growth?
faqs.a: Options include impact-oriented equity, revenue-based financing, debt from mission-aligned lenders, recoverable grants, program-related investments and blended structures that combine philanthropic and commercial capital. The right mix depends on the business model, growth timeline and how much control the founders want to retain. Investor alignment with the mission matters as much as terms, because investor expectations shape future decisions.

services.name: Customer Strategy
services.meta_description: Customer strategy consulting grounded in jobs-to-be-done research and needs-based segmentation, with frontline teams equipped to deliver on every promise.
services.summary: Understand what customers are trying to achieve, decide which customers to serve best, and align the organization to deliver on it.
services.lede: Our customer strategy consulting helps organizations understand the jobs customers are trying to get done, choose the segments and value propositions to prioritize, and align teams, processes and employee experience to deliver consistently.
challenge: Many organizations claim to be customer-centric but make decisions based on internal convenience, product features or historical segments. Customer research sits in separate pockets across marketing, product and service teams, rarely synthesized into a shared view. Segmentation is based on demographics or account size rather than needs and behaviors. As a result, organizations try to serve everyone equally, value propositions blur, and investments in channels or features are made without a clear understanding of what customers actually value.

Customer experience is also shaped by employees, yet customer strategy often ignores them. Frontline staff are asked to deliver a promised experience without the tools, authority, training or staffing to do so. Policies designed to control cost create friction that employees must explain to frustrated customers. The connection between employee experience and customer experience is well established in service research. Customer strategy consulting must account for the operating realities and people who determine whether customer promises are kept.

approach.title: Understanding customer needs in depth
approach.body: We conduct in-depth interviews, contextual observation and jobs-to-be-done research to understand what customers are trying to accomplish, the circumstances that trigger a purchase or service request, and the anxieties and trade-offs involved. Frontline employee interviews provide a parallel view of where customers struggle and what employees wish they could do differently.

approach.title: Quantifying needs and value
approach.body: We validate qualitative insights through surveys and analysis of transaction, behavioral, complaint and retention data. Needs-based segmentation identifies distinct customer groups by the outcomes they seek, and customer lifetime value and cost-to-serve analysis show the economics of each segment. Journey analytics identify where customers drop off, complain or require repeated contact.

approach.title: Choosing where and how to win
approach.body: We help leadership decide which segments to prioritize, define a differentiated value proposition for each and identify the critical moments where the experience must excel. We design the customer experience principles, service standards and supporting employee experience, testing concepts with customers and frontline staff before committing resources.

approach.title: Aligning the organization
approach.body: We translate the customer strategy into initiatives across product, marketing, sales, service and operations, with clear owners and metrics. Frontline employees receive the training, decision authority and tools needed to deliver the promised experience. Policies and processes that create unnecessary friction are redesigned, and incentives are aligned with customer outcomes rather than activity volume.

approach.title: Listening continuously
approach.body: We set up a customer insight system that combines relationship and transactional feedback, operational data and frontline insight, with governance that routes findings to owners and tracks action. Customer and employee experience metrics are reviewed together in leadership routines, so the organization notices changing needs early and adjusts before customers leave.

Value propositions and priority segment choices

outcomes: A shared, evidence-based understanding of what different customers need and value.
Investment focused on the segments and moments that matter most to growth.

services.who_we_serve: We work with chief executives, chief customer and marketing officers, product and service leaders, and operating partners in retail, financial services, healthcare, hospitality, technology and professional services, including investor-backed businesses and mission-driven organizations. Common triggers include declining retention or satisfaction, a new competitor, entry into new markets, a value creation plan that depends on customer growth, a digital transformation, or recognition that customer insight is fragmented across functions and not shaping decisions.
services.impact_lens: A thoughtful customer strategy treats customers as people with goals, constraints and dignity, not only as revenue. Customers gain products and services that fit their lives, with less friction and clearer communication. Employees gain the authority and support to solve problems rather than enforce rules they cannot explain. When strategy deliberately includes underserved customers, organizations can expand access and inclusion while building loyalty that supports durable financial performance.

faqs.q: What is jobs-to-be-done?
faqs.a: Jobs-to-be-done is a framework for understanding customer behavior based on the progress people are trying to make in a particular circumstance, rather than their demographic characteristics or product features. It examines functional, emotional and social dimensions of the job, along with the forces that encourage or prevent switching. It helps organizations design offerings and experiences around what customers are actually trying to achieve.

faqs.q: What is the difference between customer strategy and customer experience?
faqs.a: Customer strategy determines which customers to serve, what value proposition to offer each and how the organization will differentiate. Customer experience concerns how customers perceive their interactions across the journey. Strategy sets direction for experience design; experience design and operations make the strategy real. Without strategy, experience investments are scattered. Without good experience delivery, strategy remains an aspiration.

faqs.q: How does employee experience affect customer experience?
faqs.a: Employees who have the tools, information, training, authority and workload to do their jobs well are better able to serve customers. Service research has long linked employee engagement and capability to customer satisfaction and loyalty. In practice, many customer pain points trace back to internal problems, such as policies, systems or staffing, that employees experience first and can often help solve.

faqs.q: What is needs-based segmentation?
faqs.a: Needs-based segmentation groups customers by the outcomes they seek and the circumstances they are in, rather than only by demographics, firmographics or spending. It typically combines qualitative research with survey and behavioral data to identify segments with distinct priorities. Because each segment values different things, it supports sharper value propositions, product decisions and experience design than traditional segmentation.

services.name: Innovation Strategy
services.meta_description: Innovation strategy consulting to balance your portfolio of bets, set evidence-based funding gates and build the team conditions that turn ideas into results.
services.summary: Build an innovation portfolio, process and culture that consistently turn real customer and community needs into new value.
services.lede: Our innovation strategy consulting helps leaders decide where to innovate, balance a portfolio of core, adjacent and new bets, and build the processes, governance and team conditions that turn ideas into results.
challenge: Innovation efforts often generate activity without results. Organizations run idea challenges, establish labs or fund pilots, but projects remain stuck in experimentation, lack a path to scale or are disconnected from strategic priorities. Funding follows the annual budget cycle, which favors predictable projects over uncertain ones. Leaders struggle to compare initiatives at different stages, so the portfolio becomes either too conservative to matter or too scattered to sustain, and promising ideas fail to secure owners in the core business.

The deeper challenges are human. Teams may lack the psychological safety to propose untested ideas or report failed experiments honestly. Middle managers, measured on current performance, have little incentive to release people for innovation work. Innovation teams can become isolated from the operations that must eventually adopt their work. And new products are sometimes designed without meaningful input from the customers and communities they are intended to serve. Innovation strategy consulting must address incentives, culture and the people who will carry ideas forward.

approach.title: Finding unmet needs and internal barriers
approach.body: We conduct research with customers, non-customers and communities to identify unmet needs and emerging behaviors, and interview leaders, innovators and operational managers about how ideas currently move or stall. A short employee survey assesses innovation climate, including psychological safety, resource availability and leadership support for experimentation.

approach.title: Assessing the portfolio and capabilities
approach.body: We inventory current innovation initiatives and map them across core, adjacent and transformational horizons, assessing stage, investment, strategic fit and evidence of customer demand. We also assess innovation capabilities, such as research, prototyping, venture processes, partnerships and metrics, identifying where the system breaks down between idea generation and scaled adoption.

approach.title: Defining the innovation strategy and system
approach.body: We help leaders define strategic innovation priorities and the desired portfolio balance, then design the innovation system: stage-gate or venture-style funding, evidence criteria at each stage, governance, team structures and pathways from pilot to scale. Human-centered design and lean experimentation methods are embedded so teams test assumptions with real users early.

approach.title: Launching and building capability
approach.body: We support the first cycle of the new process, coaching teams through discovery, prototyping and experimentation on priority opportunities. Leaders and managers learn how to sponsor innovation, evaluate evidence and make continue, pivot or stop decisions. We help create incentives and time allocations that enable people across the organization to participate meaningfully.

approach.title: Governing and learning
approach.body: We establish innovation portfolio reviews, leading indicators such as learning velocity and validated assumptions, and lagging indicators such as adoption and revenue from new offerings. Lessons from stopped projects are captured and shared. This governance keeps innovation connected to strategy and ensures the portfolio evolves as markets, technologies and customer needs change.

Innovation climate assessment and employee survey findings
Portfolio map across core, adjacent and transformational horizons
Innovation strategy, priorities and target portfolio balance
Stage-based funding, governance and scale-up pathway design
Innovation team coaching and leadership sponsor training
outcomes: An innovation portfolio clearly connected to strategic priorities and real customer needs.
Faster, evidence-based decisions about whether to continue, pivot or stop initiatives.
Teams that feel safe proposing ideas, testing assumptions and sharing what they learn.
Clear pathways for promising pilots to scale within the core business.
services.who_we_serve: We work with chief executives, chief innovation and strategy officers, product leaders, research and development heads and innovation teams in companies, health systems, universities, financial institutions and mission-driven organizations. Common triggers include stagnating growth, disruptive competitors or technologies, an innovation lab that has not produced scaled results, a new strategic plan requiring new offerings, or board interest in a more disciplined approach to innovation investment and governance.
services.impact_lens: Innovation shapes which problems get solved and for whom. When grounded in research with customers and communities, including those often overlooked, new products and services can expand access and address unmet needs. Employees gain opportunities to contribute ideas, learn new skills and work in environments where experimentation is valued. A disciplined portfolio uses resources responsibly, and innovation that creates social as well as commercial value strengthens the organization's long-term relevance.

faqs.q: What is an innovation portfolio?
faqs.a: An innovation portfolio is the set of innovation initiatives an organization is pursuing, managed as a whole rather than project by project. Portfolios are commonly categorized by horizon or ambition, from improvements to the core business through adjacent opportunities to transformational bets. Managing them as a portfolio helps leaders balance risk and return, allocate resources deliberately and ensure the mix fits the strategy.

faqs.q: How do you measure innovation?
faqs.a: Effective innovation measurement uses different metrics by stage. Early-stage initiatives are measured on learning: assumptions tested, customer evidence gathered and speed of iteration. Later stages are measured on adoption, revenue, cost savings or impact. Applying mature business metrics to early ideas tends to end promising work prematurely, while never applying them allows weak initiatives to continue indefinitely.

faqs.q: Why do innovation labs often fail to deliver results?
faqs.a: Common reasons include isolation from the core business, unclear mandates, lack of sustained funding, no pathway to scale and incentives that discourage operational leaders from adopting new ideas. Labs succeed more often when they work on strategic priorities, involve business owners from the start, use clear evidence criteria and have agreed routes for transferring successful work into operations.

faqs.q: How does psychological safety affect innovation?
faqs.a: Innovation requires people to propose untested ideas, admit uncertainty and report failures honestly. Research on psychological safety, notably Amy Edmondson's work, shows that teams who believe they will not be punished for speaking up are more likely to learn and experiment. Leaders build it by inviting input, responding constructively to bad news and treating well-designed failed experiments as useful learning.

services.name: Responsible AI Adoption
services.meta_title: Responsible AI Adoption and Workforce Transition
services.meta_description: Responsible AI adoption: risk-based governance, task-level job redesign and fair workforce transition, so AI improves work and service without eroding trust.
services.summary: Adopt AI with clear governance, fair workforce transition and redesigned work, so productivity gains also earn employee and customer trust.
services.lede: Our responsible AI adoption services help leaders choose valuable use cases, set governance proportionate to risk, redesign jobs and workflows, and prepare employees for change, so AI improves work and service rather than eroding trust.
challenge: Organizations face pressure to adopt AI quickly, from boards, investors, competitors and employees already using tools informally. Many respond with scattered pilots that never scale, or with broad deployments lacking clear governance. Questions about data privacy, accuracy, bias, intellectual property and accountability remain unanswered. Regulatory expectations are evolving across jurisdictions. Without a deliberate approach, organizations either move too slowly to realize value or move too quickly and create risks that harm customers, employees and reputation.

The workforce dimension is often the least prepared. Employees worry about job security and whether AI will be used to monitor them. Managers do not know how to redesign roles or evaluate AI-assisted work. Expertise and judgment that took years to build may be undervalued or lost. When AI decisions affect hiring, performance or customer eligibility, fairness concerns become acute. Responsible AI adoption requires treating workforce transition, job design and employee voice as central parts of the program, not as communications afterthoughts.

approach.title: Understanding work and concerns
approach.body: We interview leaders, managers and employees across functions to understand current AI use, including informal use, the tasks people find most burdensome and their concerns about AI. Customer and, where relevant, worker representative perspectives are included. This research identifies use cases grounded in real work and surfaces trust issues that adoption must address.

approach.title: Assessing tasks, risks and readiness
approach.body: We conduct a task-level analysis of priority roles to identify which activities AI could automate, augment or leave unchanged, and assess data readiness, risk level and potential value of candidate use cases. A risk tiering approach, informed by frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, determines the level of oversight each use case requires.

approach.title: Designing governance, work and transition
approach.body: We design an AI governance model with policies, review processes, accountability and human oversight proportionate to risk. For priority use cases, we redesign workflows and roles with the employees involved, defining where human judgment remains essential. A workforce transition plan covers reskilling, redeployment, new roles and commitments about how productivity gains will be shared.

approach.title: Piloting and scaling responsibly
approach.body: We support pilots with clear success criteria, including quality, fairness, employee experience and customer outcomes alongside productivity. Training builds AI literacy for all employees and deeper skills for those whose roles change most. Managers learn to lead hybrid human and AI work. Successful pilots scale through a structured process that includes impact assessment and change management.

approach.title: Monitoring and adapting

services.impact_lens: AI will reshape work for many people, and how organizations adopt it matters. A responsible approach protects employees through reskilling, transparent communication and fair sharing of gains. Customers benefit from AI that is accurate, fair and subject to meaningful human oversight. Communities benefit when organizations avoid deploying systems that reinforce bias or exclusion. And careful adoption builds the trust that lets organizations realize lasting productivity and service improvements from AI.

faqs.q: What is responsible AI?
faqs.a: Responsible AI refers to developing and using artificial intelligence in ways that are safe, fair, transparent, accountable and respectful of privacy and human rights. In practice, it involves governance policies, risk assessment, human oversight, testing for bias and accuracy, monitoring after deployment and mechanisms for people affected by AI decisions to understand and challenge them. It also includes attention to how AI affects workers.

faqs.q: How should organizations govern AI use?
faqs.a: Effective AI governance is proportionate to risk. It typically includes an inventory of AI use, a risk tiering process, policies for acceptable use and data handling, review requirements for higher-risk uses, clear accountability, human oversight and monitoring. Frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the ISO/IEC AI management system standard provide useful structure. Governance should enable valuable use, not only restrict it.

faqs.q: How can we prepare our workforce for AI?
faqs.a: Start with honest communication about intentions and how gains will be shared. Analyze roles at the task level to understand likely changes, then design reskilling and redeployment pathways. Build AI literacy for everyone and deeper skills for roles that change most. Involve employees in redesigning workflows, because they understand the work and its risks. Train managers to lead teams through the transition.

faqs.q: Will AI replace jobs in our organization?
faqs.a: AI typically changes tasks within jobs before it changes the jobs themselves, automating some activities, augmenting others and creating new ones. The net effect depends on your strategy and choices, including whether productivity gains are used to reduce headcount, grow the business or improve service. We help leaders analyze likely impacts by role and make deliberate, transparent decisions about workforce transition.

services.name: Talent Strategy
services.meta_description: Talent strategy consulting that links critical capabilities to an evidence-based employee value proposition, career architecture and fair internal mobility.
services.summary: Align how you attract, develop, deploy and retain people with your business strategy, built on evidence and a compelling employee value proposition.
services.lede: Our talent strategy consulting helps leaders define the capabilities their strategy requires, build an employee value proposition people believe, and design hiring, development, mobility and retention practices that deliver the right talent.
challenge: Many organizations manage talent through a collection of HR programs, recruiting campaigns, training catalogs, performance processes and compensation reviews, each managed separately and rarely connected to strategy. When the business shifts, such as entering new markets, adopting new technology or changing its operating model, talent practices lag behind. Critical roles remain vacant, skills gaps grow, high performers leave for clearer opportunities elsewhere and costly external hiring becomes the default response to every capability need.

Employees experience the gap directly. The promises made in recruitment do not match the reality of the job. Career paths are unclear, internal moves are harder than external ones, and development depends on which manager you happen to have. Groups of employees may face different barriers to advancement. Talent strategy consulting must connect the business need for capabilities with what employees need to join, grow and stay, using evidence rather than assumptions about what people value.

approach.title: Understanding what people value
approach.body: We interview leaders about strategic capability needs and conduct focus groups and interviews with employees across levels, including recent hires and leavers, about why they joined, stay or leave. Candidate perspectives reveal how the organization is perceived in the talent market. This research forms the basis of an authentic employee value proposition.

approach.title: Analyzing the talent system
approach.body: We analyze workforce data on hiring, internal mobility, promotion, performance, engagement, pay and attrition, disaggregated to identify differences across groups. We identify critical roles, those with outsized impact on strategy, and assess supply, risk and skills gaps. Labor market analysis shows competition for key skills and realistic expectations for building versus buying talent.

approach.title: Building the talent strategy
approach.body: We define the capabilities required by the strategy, a build, buy, borrow and redeploy approach for each critical capability and an employee value proposition grounded in research. We then design aligned practices, such as skills-based hiring, career architecture, an internal talent marketplace, leadership development and targeted retention, testing proposals with employees and managers.

approach.title: Implementing priority practices
approach.body: We support implementation of priority initiatives, including employer brand updates consistent with the EVP, career framework rollout, manager training on development conversations and internal mobility processes. We work with HR, finance and business leaders to align budgets and accountability, and use pilots to test practices before scaling them across the organization.

approach.title: Measuring talent outcomes
approach.body: We establish a talent dashboard tracking leading and lagging indicators such as critical role coverage, internal fill rate, quality of hire, regretted attrition, development participation and equity of outcomes. Regular talent reviews connect these measures to business planning, and periodic employee listening checks whether the value proposition matches lived experience.

Triggers include a new strategy or operating model, persistent hiring difficulties for critical roles, rising regretted attrition, an acquisition combining different talent practices, adoption of AI changing skill requirements, employer brand challenges, or a board request for a clearer view of talent risk and capability.
services.impact_lens: Talent strategy determines who gets opportunity inside an organization. Employees gain clear career paths, fair access to development and a workplace that matches its promises. Customers benefit from capable, engaged employees who stay long enough to build expertise and relationships. Inclusive hiring and mobility practices can open opportunity to people historically excluded from good jobs. And a talent system aligned with strategy supports performance that sustains employment and investment.

faqs.q: What is an employee value proposition?
faqs.a: An employee value proposition, or EVP, describes the total value employees receive in exchange for their work, including compensation, benefits, career growth, work environment, culture, purpose and flexibility. A strong EVP is grounded in research with current employees and candidates, differentiated from competitors for talent and honest about the experience. It guides recruitment messaging and helps prioritize investments in employee experience.

faqs.q: What is the difference between talent strategy and workforce planning?
faqs.a: Strategic workforce planning analyzes future workforce demand and supply, identifying gaps in numbers and skills over time. Talent strategy uses those insights, along with research on what people value, to decide how the organization will attract, develop, deploy and retain talent. Workforce planning answers what talent you need; talent strategy answers how you will secure and grow it.

faqs.q: What does build, buy, borrow mean in talent strategy?
faqs.a: It is a framework for closing capability gaps. Build means developing existing employees through training, experience and mobility. Buy means hiring externally. Borrow means using contractors, partners or temporary talent. Many organizations also consider redeployment, moving people from roles with declining demand to roles with growing demand, and automation. The right mix depends on time, cost, risk and the strategic importance of the capability.

faqs.q: How do you identify critical roles?
faqs.a: Critical roles are those with a disproportionate effect on strategy execution, customer outcomes or risk, not necessarily the most senior roles. We assess roles by strategic impact, performance variability, difficulty of replacement and supply in the labor market. Critical roles then receive focused attention in succession, development, retention and workforce planning, so the organization concentrates effort where it matters most.
